cleanParagraphs: After the storm, Noah and Ms. Rivera arrived at the planetarium to prepare the evening event. They found that the control-room door was locked and the main power was off. Noah tried the handle, but it did not move. Instead of forcing it, they searched the old duty records for a safe way inside.

One note said a spare key rested behind a labeled cabinet near the front desk. Noah found it and gave it to Ms. Rivera, who called Dr. Hall before they entered. The administrator confirmed the safety steps. Inside, they saw a wet fuse box below a leaking pipe, and Ms. Rivera marked the area immediately.

When power returned, lights on the console flashed repeatedly, but the dome stayed still. Noah watched the live voltage display and said, “The reading is changing now, and the warning light is getting brighter.” Ms. Rivera checked the normal operating guide. “The voltage usually stays steady,” she explained, “and this light normally turns off after startup.”

Noah looked through the vent. “The cooling fan is not turning at the moment, although it normally turns whenever the system runs. This pattern repeats every time we start the system,” he added. Rather than force the dome control, they chose to repair the fan first, because rising heat could damage the equipment.

Mina arrived with dry cloths, insulated tools, and a portable air blower. Together, the three team members cleaned the fuse box and reconnected the cooling fan. When the blades began turning, Noah checked his list. “We have dried the box, and Mina has inspected every damp connection,” he reported carefully.

“We have reconnected the fan, but we have not tested the dome sensor yet. The warning light has gone off, so the repairs have given us a stable result. The latest evidence has shown us that the main system can enter a low-power test,” Ms. Rivera said. However, the sensor still needed a separate check before the dome moved.

On a video call, Dr. Hall explained the requirements before the sensor test. “You must clear the entire dome track, and everyone has to stand behind the yellow line. Noah, you have to confirm that the emergency stop button responds.” The team followed each instruction slowly. Mina marked checked areas with removable tags while Ms. Rivera watched the camera feed.

Before they could begin, Noah noticed a repair ladder beside the track. “We must not start while this is here. The test has to wait until every hazard is gone. We have to move it beyond the safety line, and I must check the stop button again.” They paused, carried the ladder to the storage room, and repeated the inspection.

Before the final test, Noah compared two plans aloud. “If the sensor passes, we will open the planetarium as planned. If it fails again, we will hold a small star-map lesson instead.” Then he considered a less likely problem: “If the dome were to stop halfway, we would keep visitors in the classroom and use the backup lesson.”

The sensor test began. “If the green light appears, the system will be ready,” Ms. Rivera said. The light appeared, and the dome opened after the team checked the track again. Noah smiled. “If we skipped the safety steps, we would create danger. If the weather changes, we will use the backup lesson.” Visitors arrived on time.

mainIdea.text: After a storm disables the planetarium, Noah and Ms. Rivera use an old duty record and Dr. Hall's safety guidance to enter the locked control room. They find a wet fuse box and restore power, but live readings show that the cooling fan is not working normally. Mina brings drying tools, and the team cleans the box, reconnects the fan, and reports what it has repaired. Because the dome sensor still needs testing, they use a low-power check instead of forcing the system. They clear the track, remain behind the safety line, test the emergency stop, and remove a forgotten ladder. They compare a normal opening with a star-map backup plan. When the sensor passes, the dome opens safely, and the event begins on time.
